title: Products
jupyter: python3
---

In Starsim, a **product** represents the actual medical tool that an intervention delivers: a diagnostic test, a treatment, or a vaccine. The split between *interventions* and *products* mirrors how real programs work: an intervention decides *who* gets something and *when* (eligibility, coverage, timing), while the product defines *what* happens to an agent when it's administered.

This separation means you can reuse the same product across different delivery strategies. For example, a single vaccine product can be deployed via a routine immunization program in one scenario and a one-off campaign in another, without redefining the vaccine itself.

For how products are *delivered*, see the [Interventions](modules_interventions.qmd) page; this page focuses on the products themselves.

## Product types

There are three products, one for each kind of delivery:

| Class | Represents | Delivered by | Main arguments |
|-------|------------|--------------|----------------|
| `ss.Vaccine` | Vaccines | `ss.vaccinate()` | `efficacy`, `waning`, `leaky`, `cost` |
| `ss.Diagnostic` | Diagnostics | `ss.screen()` | `sensitivity`, `specificity`, `delay`, `detects`, `cost` |
| `ss.Treatment` | Treatments | `ss.treat()` | `cure`, `efficacy`, `transition`, `cost` |

They work with every solver: in an agent-based run the sim records who holds a product and since when, and in a compartmental run holding it becomes a stratification of the model.

## Vaccines

A vaccine's `efficacy` is its protection against acquisition: everyone who holds it has their susceptibility (`rel_sus`) multiplied by `1 - efficacy`. A dict gives efficacy against several things at once: `acquisition` (scales `rel_sus`), `transmission` (scales `rel_trans`), `mortality` (scales the disease's death transitions), the name of any transition in the disease (which scales its rate, or its probability if it is a branch chosen with `p=`), or one destination of a transition with several, as `'<transition>.<state>'` (`efficacy={'progression.C': 0.5}` halves the chance of going to `C` without changing how long people take to leave). `waning` is how protection fades with time since delivery: a duration means protection is lost after an exponentially distributed time with that mean. With `leaky=False`, the vaccine is "all or nothing": a fraction `efficacy` of those vaccinated are fully protected and the rest are not protected at all.

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

pars = dict(n_agents=5000, start='2000', stop='2020', diseases=ss.SIS(), networks='random', verbose=0)

leaky  = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8)                        # Everyone vaccinated is 80% protected
aon    = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8, leaky=False)           # 80% of those vaccinated are fully protected
waning = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8, waning=ss.years(3))    # Protection is lost after 3 years on average

kw = dict(coverage=0.5, at=['2010'])
msim = ss.parallel(
    baseline = ss.Sim(**pars),
    leaky    = ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=ss.vaccinate(leaky, **kw)),
    aon      = ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=ss.vaccinate(aon, **kw)),
    waning   = ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=ss.vaccinate(waning, **kw)),
)
msim.plot('sis.prevalence')
```

A product is realized as modifiers on the people who hold it, so it combines with other modifiers by the usual rule: two vaccines against acquisition multiply, and both are listed by `sim.what_modifies(sis.rel_sus)`.

## Tests

A test is defined by its `sensitivity` (the probability that someone with the condition tests positive) and `specificity` (the probability that someone without it tests negative). By default it detects infection with the disease it is delivered for; `detects=` takes a condition to say something else. `delay=` is the time from the test to its result. What happens to the people who test positive is a follow-up delivery, given them with `who=screening.positive`:

```{python}
test = ss.Diagnostic(sensitivity=0.95, specificity=0.99)
drug = ss.Treatment(cure=0.9)
screening = ss.screen(test, coverage=0.5, interval=ss.years(1), start='2010')
treatment = ss.treat(drug, who=screening.positive)

sim = ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=[screening, treatment])
sim.run()
sim.plot('sis')
print(f'Positive tests: {sim.results.screening.positive.sum():n}')
```

## Treatments

`cure=` is the probability that treatment clears the infection, once, when it is given: the person leaves the infected states by the disease's recovery transition (`transition=` names it when there are several). `efficacy=`, a dict as for vaccines, is what the treatment does while it is held, such as antiretroviral therapy (`efficacy=dict(transmission=0.96, mortality=0.9)`); the two can be given together. A treatment is given to the people who are infected, unless `eligible=` says otherwise.

Here infection is cleared with 80% efficacy, with at most 300 treatments in each yearly round from 2010:

```{python}
drug = ss.Treatment(cure=0.8)
treatment = ss.treat(drug, interval=ss.years(1), start='2010', capacity=300)

msim = ss.parallel(
    no_treatment = ss.Sim(**pars),
    treatment    = ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=treatment),
)
msim.plot('sis.n_I')
```

`capacity=` caps how many people can be treated: a bare number is per round (or per step, for delivery on events), and a rate such as `ss.peryear(300)` is per unit time, which is how a capacity is given to routine delivery.

## Costs

Every product takes `cost=`, the cost of each delivery. The cost is then a result of the delivery, alongside the number delivered, which is all that is needed for a simple cost-effectiveness comparison:

```{python}
vaccine = ss.Vaccine(efficacy=0.8, cost=12.50)
vaccination = ss.vaccinate(vaccine, coverage=0.5, at=['2010'])
sim = ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=vaccination)
sim.run()
res = sim.results.vaccination
print(f'Doses: {res.delivered.sum():n}; total cost: ${res.cost.sum():,.2f}')
```

## Tests with several results, and treatment queues

A test can have more than two results: `results=` gives them most severe first, each with its probability for people in each state (`None` for people in none of the states), and the last result is `None`, everyone the others do not take. Each result is a result of the delivery and an event that can trigger what follows; `positive` is any result but the last. A treatment can have a capacity, and with `queue=True` those not served wait, longest first, until they are served or are no longer eligible (a duration, e.g. `queue=ss.months(6)`, limits the wait):

```{python}
cytology = ss.Diagnostic(results=dict(high=dict(I=0.9), low={'I': 0.05, None: 0.02}, normal=None)) # Low grade for 2% of those not infected
screening = ss.screen(cytology, coverage=0.5, start='2010', interval=ss.years(1))
treatment = ss.treat(ss.Treatment(cure=0.8), who=screening.high, capacity=50, queue=True) # At most 50 treated each step

sim = ss.Sim(**pars, interventions=[screening, treatment])
sim.run()
res = sim.results
print(f'High grade: {res.screening.high.sum():n}; low grade: {res.screening.low.sum():n}; treated: {res.treatment.delivered.sum():n}')
```

A product whose effect needs code of its own, such as a protection computed for each agent, is an intervention written as code (see [Interventions](modules_interventions.qmd#writing-an-intervention-as-code)); an effect on the people who hold a product can also be a modifier whose `where=` is the product's memory, e.g. `ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=0.5, where=vaccine.since > ss.years(5))`.

:::{.callout-tip}
Because products are modules, they can define their own parameters (with `define_pars()`), states, and results, just like any other Starsim module. See [Adding new modules](modules_adding.qmd) for the general pattern.
:::
